source.title: The Linear Centroids Hypothesis: Features as Directions Learned by Local Experts
source.authors: Thomas Walker; Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun; Randall Balestriero; R. Baraniuk

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites polysemantic neurons as context for circuit research, but does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether their meanings are coherent.
record.gate_note: The discussion of polysemantic neurons is background attributed to prior work, not a result of this study. The GPT2-Large neuron-attribution experiment measures a neuron's contribution to a local mapping for one prompt; it does not measure semantic response diversity.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a centroid-based interpretability framework. Polysemantic neurons appear only in Appendix C, which describes why Olah et al. introduced circuits. No result measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, or the causes, prevalence or measurement dependence of that. The GPT2-Large experiment ranks one neuron's attribution on one prompt.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that replacing activations with centroids (Jacobian row-sums) gives a mapping-aware drop-in for interpretability tools. They report sparser, more transferable SAE dictionaries, resistance to spurious features, circuit discovery via centroid attribution, and faithful saliency maps.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Jacobian-derived centroids and a centroid-attribution metric, rather than testing neuron polysemanticity with the original sources' methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Centroid-based attribution placed GPT2-Large layer-31 neuron 892 (the 'an' neuron) at the 99.8th percentile for one prompt neighbourhood. The percentile was stable across neighbourhood sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Centroid-perturbation attribution can isolate functionally relevant neurons in a given prompt context.

record.problems: The study does not measure polysemanticity. Its neuron-attribution example uses one prompt context and cannot establish whether a neuron has one coherent job or responds to unrelated inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were left out. Other reported comparisons concern centroid-based feature dictionaries, probes, saliency, or attribution-method robustness rather than neuron semantic response diversity.

untested.parts: Whether vision-classifier neurons respond to several unrelated inputs.
Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models, and how it varies by layer.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Effect of architecture, activation function or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons.
Whether apparently polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or on how explanations are scored.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. Polysemanticity is mentioned once as background attributed to Zoom In, one of the original sources. Appendix F's qualitative remark that LCH SAE features are 'more semantically coherent' concerns SAE features, not neurons, so it bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether vision-model neurons respond to multiple unrelated inputs.
Whether language-model MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how prevalence varies by layer.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether architecture, activation, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons, or reduces it without substantial performance loss.
Whether apparently polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related features when examined with better tools.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: GPT2-Large
rows.operation_detail: Applied the centroid-based neuron-attribution metric to a neighborhood of last-token embeddings at layer 31.

conditions.value: “I climbed up the pear tree and picked a pear. I climbed up the apple tree and picked.”

rows.measure: Neuron attribution percentile in the layer's distribution
rows.value: The 892nd neuron was in the top 99.8th percentile.
rows.note: This reports attribution for one prompt context, not whether the neuron responds to several unrelated inputs.
rows.check: This row is a demonstration of the study's own attribution method: it recovers a neuron known from prior work, on one prompt. It measures no neuron response diversity, so it should not count as a claim-relevant result row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
